newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: N.Zealand monetary easing out of question - Westpac.
newsitem.headline: N.Zealand monetary easing out of question - Westpac.

text.p: An explicit easing of monetary policy by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand is out of the question at this time, Westpac Bank said in its Weekly commentary released on Friday.
The bank was commenting on the Reserve Bank's Economic Projections due on Friday September 13.

"The Reserve Bank will not want any market reaction nor change in monetary conditions from this announcement. They may still comment that a change in the mix of monetary conditions could be desirable (higher interest rates and a lower exchange rate), but an explicit easing is out of the question at this

Westpac did not anticipate any significant changes in the Reserve Bank's inflation projections and expected the Reserve Bank would assume monetary conditions remained broadly in line with the recent mix of conditions.
"We believe that it is still too early for the Reserve Bank to be entirely comfortable with the outlook for underlying inflation," the bank said.

"The fact is that the Reserve Bank simply does not know how much of any apparent slowing in the rate of expansion of the domestic economy is being driven by current monetary conditions, or in fact a holding period before the election as consumers/investors/businesses employ a 'wait and see' strategy."
The data for an easing on monetary conditions was likely to be more convincing by October or November, the bank said.
"Financial markets will anticipate this easing as the weaker economic data comes to hand; therefore interest rates will tend to have a downward bias from now on."
Westpac expected the bank to reiterate that an easing in monetary conditions would be appropriate in due course provided inflation continued to track according to forecasts.

Areas for concern for the Reserve Bank had been the continued growth in the labour market, with still no clear direction for unit labour costs, the bank said. Although housing market activity had slowed from frenetic pace earlier in the year, Westpac thought it premature to assume that the current cycle in property prices and construction activity had peaked.

"Finally there is the impact of the tax cuts...(Although), the Reserve Bank still anticipated 'a sizable boost to aggregate demand', ....it appears monetary policy remains sufficiently firm to offset much of the stimulus that would have been expected from the tax cuts."
